method: Descriptions authored after inspecting the retained ten scene contact sheets; L1.8 wording reflects the corrected derivative. No claim of full-frame human acceptance.

1: The recurring manufacturing-system diagram links people and equipment to a controlled process and product quality.
The coloured three-by-three risk matrix is illustrative. It communicates increasing relative risk; its numbers and colours are not a universal scoring standard.
The quality-system slides connect oversight, accountability, personnel training and process controls.
Process flow runs from input through process, monitoring and review; testing alone cannot build quality into a product.
The vessel illustration marks equipment identification and calibration/status checks. Verify identity, cleaning and relevant instrument calibration before use.
Documentation flow links approved instructions to execution records and review. Instructions state what to do; records show what occurred.
Deviation and change-control illustrations reinforce recording, assessment and authorized decisions.
2: Quality system: people, processes and oversight work together.
Management responsibility: lead, resource and review.
Risk management: assess, control and review, proportionate to product impact.
Deviation/CAPA: document, investigate and verify effectiveness.
Change management: propose, assess and approve before implementation.
Data integrity: attribute, preserve and retrieve complete, trustworthy records.
Expired calibration example: hold, assess and document; evaluate instrument status and product impact.
3: Personnel responsibilities: understand, perform and report.
Training: train, demonstrate competence and reassess; attendance alone is insufficient.
Hygiene: hand hygiene, appropriate clothing and reporting relevant conditions.
Gowning: prepare, gown and verify according to the area-specific procedure.
Controlled-area behaviour: follow flows, minimize risk and escalate concerns.
Contamination prevention: identify, segregate and verify materials and status.
Supervision: supervise, document and review actual work.
Missed gowning step: stop, report and assess under the approved procedure.
4: Premises: design, maintain and monitor for the intended process.
Material/personnel flow: receive, control movement and produce while preventing contamination and mix-ups.
Cleaning: follow the procedure, clean and verify effectiveness.
Equipment design connects suitable materials, cleanability and intended use.
Calibration and maintenance: calibrate, maintain and record; assess overdue work.
Qualification: IQ, OQ and PQ mean installation, operational and performance qualification. Scope and acceptance criteria are system-specific.
Status: identify equipment, check status and record; labels complement controlled records.
Expired calibration: hold, report and assess. The revised scenario concerns a measuring instrument used with a vessel, not calibration of the vessel itself.
5: Manufacturing control: approved instructions, execution and review.
Material status has distinct quarantine, released and rejected states. Verify records, not only container labels.
Dispensing connects material identity, measurement and recording. Perform applicable independent checks and maintain batch traceability.
Line clearance: clear the area, check setup and authorize the operation under approved procedures.
In-process control loop: measure, compare with approved limits, then respond and record.
Batch records connect operations, in-process data and reconciliation; investigate unexplained gaps.
Deviation response: secure, report and assess while preserving evidence.
Conflicting status: a released label and a system hold are inconsistent. Hold the material and escalate; do not select the preferred status.
6: Pack identity links product, carton and label; mismatch can affect patient safety.
Printed materials: approve, issue and reconcile; segregate obsolete artwork.
Line clearance: remove previous materials, verify equipment and record checks.
In-process packaging checks cover identity, print and pack integrity.
Traceability links unit pack, carton and shipper through identifiers and records.
Reconciliation compares issued material with material accounted for: used, rejected, returned or another documented disposition. Investigate unexplained differences.
Mix-up barriers: segregate, identify, verify and review.
Wrong-strength carton: stop, report and assess; resume only after authorized disposition and preserve evidence.
7: Quality control: sample, analyze and review. Testing supports GMP controls.
Specification control links method, test and approved criteria.
Sampling chain of custody: identify the sample, control handling and trace analysis.
Instrument readiness covers calibration, suitability and records.
OOS response: preserve the original result, investigate and assess impact. Retesting requires justification and approval.
Laboratory integrity includes raw data, metadata and audit trails.
Batch disposition integrates records, testing and deviations before an authorized release decision.
Failed-assay example: preserve, report, investigate and decide. Do not replace a failing result without justification.
8: Deviation management: detect, assess and prevent recurrence.
Containment: stop or secure as appropriate, segregate and preserve evidence; report under site procedures.
Deviation record: what, when and where; affected material; immediate action.
Root-cause investigation considers people, process and equipment. The corrected slide says investigate root causes.
Product impact review considers batch scope, risk evidence and disposition.
CAPA links correction and prevention to demonstrated causes, assigned owners and verified implementation.
Effectiveness review: implement, monitor, trend and verify that controls work.
Pressure alarm example: report, preserve, assess and verify. A return to normal does not erase the event.
9: Change control connects proposal, assessment and closure; evaluate change before affecting GMP operations.
Change request compares the current state, proposed state and rationale, identifying affected systems.
Impact assessment covers product quality, validation status and regulatory status.
Risk-based verification considers possible failure, controls and verification.
Approval gates: assessment and authorization precede execution.
Implementation: execute, verify and document evidence and deviations; complete needed qualification and updates.
Closure considers records, training, monitoring and residual risk.
HVAC sensor example: request, assess, calibrate and verify that replacement maintains the qualified function.
10: Internal oversight: review, identify gaps and improve before quality is affected.
Inspection plan: define scope, prioritize and assign objectively.
Prepare evidence: procedures, records and current status must reflect real operations.
Conduct inspection: observe, interview and document evidence rather than assumptions.
Findings: record facts, impact and follow-up, separating verified findings from advice.
Corrective action: establish cause, act and verify effectiveness.
Daily readiness: train, record and review continuously.
Expired-status example: secure, assess and resolve; replacing a label alone is insufficient.
